device.name: Parrot Drones (AR.Drone / Bebop / Anafi)
device.notes:
Parrot's consumer drones — AR.Drone 1.0/2.0 (AT-command era) and the Bebop/ Anafi ARSDK3 generation — are controlled entirely locally over the drone's own Wi-Fi access point, no cloud ever. Parrot exited the consumer/toy drone market in 2019 (only Anafi and its variants continued, then wound down), so the AR.Drone and Bebop lines are abandoned — a clean rescue, and unusually Parrot open-sourced the SDK.
AR.DRONE 1.0/2.0: connect to the drone AP (IP 192.168.1.1) and send AT commands over UDP port 5556 — text commands like `AT*REF=1,512\r` (takeoff/ land), with sequence numbering; plus a TCP video stream.
BEBOP/ANAFI (ARSDK3): discovery is a TCP handshake on port 44444 — the controller sends JSON {"controller_type":"computer","controller_name": "<name>","d2c_port":"43210"} and the drone replies with {"c2d_port":54321, "arstream_fragment_size":1000,...}. After that: UDP 54321 = commands (controller->drone, c2d); UDP 43210 = navdata (drone->controller, d2c). Bebop-family AP IP is 192.168.42.1. Commands are (projectId u8, classId u8, commandId u16) triples on channel 10; PCMD motion is sent ~40 Hz.

openness.notes: Parrot open-sourced the SDK (arsdk-xml, libARDiscovery, Olympe) and published protocol PDFs; AR.Drone AT commands and the ARSDK3 ports are community-documented on top. No account or cloud.

exclusivity.recovery: Close FreeFlight on every phone and switch off any SkyController before connecting. An ARSDK3 drone serves one controller at a time: a second TCP 44444 handshake is answered with the "product already connected" status (-3999 in libARDiscovery) instead of a c2d port, and the first controller keeps priority. On an AR.Drone with Pairing switched on, the drone ignores every device but the paired one — turn Pairing off from that phone, or press the Unpair button.

pairing.notes: The ARSDK3 discovery handshake authorises nothing. The controller's JSON carries a name, a type and its d2c port — no key, token or challenge — and the drone answers with status 0 and its c2d port, or a busy/not-ready status; whoever completes it first flies the drone. The only real gate is the drone's own access point. AR.Drone and Bebop ship it open (Bebop can be given a WPA2 passphrase the owner chooses in FreeFlight Pro). Anafi ships it WPA2 with a per-unit password on a label on the drone — a credential, so not recorded here — which a hard reset also writes to a text file on the microSD card, and which pairing a SkyController 3 over USB replaces with a new key. The Anafi Ai disables direct Wi-Fi to a phone or computer altogether until it is enabled in FreeFlight 7. The AR.Drone's optional Pairing restricts control to the first device's MAC address, which is a filter, not a credential. Nothing here depends on a Parrot server.

unpair.notes: Only the AR.Drone has anything to unpair. On AR.Drone 2.0 the same restriction is the Pairing option in AR.FreeFlight, switched off from the paired phone. ARSDK3 drones store no client at all; a SkyController's knowledge of an Anafi lives on the controller, and its USB pairing re-keys the drone's Wi-Fi rather than registering a client.

procedures.basis: Parrot's AR.Drone user guide, which describes an Unpair button on the underside, pressed with a pin, that erases the pairing and confirms by flashing the four LEDs red and green; community set-up guides for second-hand drones give the same step.
procedures.indicator: The four motor LEDs flash red and green.
procedures.name: AR.Drone: press the recessed Unpair button

steps.action: With the drone powered, press the recessed Unpair button on its underside with a pin.
steps.expect: The LEDs flash red and green; any phone can now connect.

credentials.notes: The drone hosts an open (or WPA) AP and has no application-layer auth: a client on the AP has full control. SAFETY: this commands flight; treat all controls as advanced.

factory_reset.description: Both routes do the same thing, and the button route is the one that matters here: it works with no vendor app at all, which is the whole reason this hardware is documented. Ten seconds on the power button of a drone that is already switched on.
factory_reset.effect: Deletes the drone's settings and preferences along with the photos and videos held in its internal memory. There is no cloud credential to clear — the media is the thing that is lost, and it is lost irreversibly, so offload it first.

procedures.basis: Parrot's Bebop 2 user guide, which gives this as the app-free equivalent of the in-app factory reset.
procedures.name: On/off button held for ten seconds

steps.action: Press and hold the on/off button for ten seconds.
steps.expect: Settings, preferences and the internal photo and video memory are erased.

methods.description: Join the drone's own Wi-Fi AP; then send AR.Drone AT commands on UDP 5556, or perform the ARSDK3 TCP 44444 discovery handshake and use the negotiated c2d/d2c UDP ports.

steps.action: Join the drone's Wi-Fi access point.
AR.Drone: send AT commands on UDP 5556. ARSDK3: TCP 44444 handshake, then UDP 54321/43210.

setup.notes: No provisioning and no account: the drone IS the access point. Join its Wi-Fi and start talking (AT commands on UDP 5556 for AR.Drone, or the TCP 44444 handshake for ARSDK3). No pairing secret.

rejoin.notes: The drone is its own AP; there is no home-network membership to change.

testing.notes: Not driven against hardware by this project. AR.Drone AT commands are from node-ar-drone; the ARSDK3 discovery handshake and UDP ports are from the katarina RE doc (Parrot's own ARSDK_Protocols.pdf is a binary PDF).
